newsitem.title: BULGARIA: INSTANT VIEW - Bulgaria pegs lev to mark at 1,000.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Bulgaria pegs lev to mark at 1,000.

text.p: Following are analysts' comments on Bulgaria Finance Minister Muravei Radev announcing the lev will be pegged to the mark as anchor in a currency board system at 1,000 levs and 1997 draft budget deficit of 6.2 percent.

DAVID BOREN, VICE PRESIDENT EMERGING MARKETS RESEARCH, SALOMON BROTHERS - I am reasonbaly confident about this exchange rate. I thought that with the market having established equilibrium at around 1,500 (levs to the dollar) it would not be required for the currency to depreciate all the way to 2,000 (as the IMF envisaged in March).

I am more concerned about the increase of the size of the budget deficit. I think that financing the budget deficit is potentially a challenge for the government given they do not want to increase significantly the domestic debt burden. It is going to place a heavier burden on the privatisation programme for financing the budget. Tangible proceeds for privatisation need to be realised as soon as possible.
The critical time is actualy two to three months after the currency board has been introduced and remains to be seen what happens to interest rates.

PARVOLETA SHTEREVA, EMERGING MARKETS ECONOMIST ING BANK LONDON - The lev/mark peg rate is a too strong level and we were looking at a level closer to 2,000 levs to the dollar. The currency is quite strong and will become stronger, because we expect the mark to strengthen against the dollar, which means the lev will become overvalued by the end of the year.
This means the government must speed up structural reform measures to justify this appreciation of the lev. If this does not happen we are going have a worsening trade balance.
The deficit is very high, this level is quite inflationary which will mean that we will not be able to see a sharp decline in interest rates.

STUART PARKINSON, EMERGING MARKETS, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL - There is more than enough money coming from official lenders now to ensure that the currency board gets a good start. We think choosing the mark as anchor makes better economic sense.

If the budget deficit is too big and cannot be controlled it can put the currency board under pressure. In order to prevent that we need to see a stronger institutional framework for framing budget policy, spending decisons, we need to see more controls.
We feel there are reasons to be confident in the near term.
